f: Collaborative culture must be embedded in processes and shared values rather than depending on specific individuals, because personal relationships are inherently fragile—they shift when people move roles, projects change phase, or new stakeholders enter the work. When relationship management becomes structural, collaboration survives these inevitable transitions.

The fragility of relationship-based collaboration becomes apparent in complex, multi-year projects. When trust exists only between two people—say, a project manager and a vendor account lead—what happens the moment one of them leaves or rotates to a different assignment? The institutional knowledge of how decisions are really made, what behaviors are expected, and how conflicts get resolved walks out the door with them.

This is why Brett Ackroyd discusses the ISO 44001 framework , which codifies collaborative behaviors and relationship management into organizational systems. Rather than relying on personalities to drive collaboration, elite delivery teams make collaboration predictable. The values—trust, transparency, mutual accountability—become documented principles that new team members inherit the moment they join, regardless of who they're replacing.
Building collaboration into the operating system, not just the people

The real work lies in examining your processes and systems to see whether they actually support the collaborative behaviors you claim to value. A team might say it believes in transparency, but if the contract structure encourages each party to hoard information for leverage in disputes, transparency will fail the moment pressure arrives.

When you design collaboration into roles, approval workflows, risk-sharing mechanisms, and reporting cadences, it survives the personnel churn that is inevitable in long-running infrastructure and government projects. A new commercial manager arriving mid-project can immediately see how decisions flow, how conflicts are escalated, and what behaviors are non-negotiable—because these are embedded in the system, not hidden in the relationships of their predecessors.

9f62155862.q: What happens when teams take a claims-focused approach instead of collaborative problem-solving?

9f62155862.e: How Collaborative Working Saves Projects | Project Management | Ep. 15
f: Australia spends more of its project budget on claims than any other Western nation , a direct result of teams prioritizing contractual leverage over collaborative problem-solving. When parties adopt a claims-focused mindset, they hold back discovered problems for future negotiation, eroding trust and making everyone defensive about contractual certainty rather than focused on achieving the shared project objective.
The Cost of Holding Back Information

In a claims-focused culture, teams treat problems as negotiating ammunition rather than shared challenges to solve together. When someone discovers an issue, instead of raising it immediately for the team's benefit, they file it away as a potential claim. This defensive posture transforms relationships from collaborative to adversarial , where each party views the other as a future opponent rather than a partner in delivery.

As Brett Ackroyd explains in the episode , this mindset makes people reluctant to expose vulnerabilities or admit they need help. Problems that could be solved quickly and cheaply spiral into expensive disputes because they were never raised in real time. The financial impact compounds across years of project execution.
The Trust Erosion Cycle

Trust is fragile in a claims-focused environment. Once teams sense that others are withholding information or waiting for an opportunity to lodge a claim, defensive behaviour spreads across the entire organisation. People become focused on protecting their contractual position rather than solving problems, which directly undermines project performance and delivery timelines.

f: Project failures rarely stem from budget, timeline, or scope alone—they emerge from teams' inability to act on problems they already know how to solve due to contractual boundaries, organisational silos, lack of authority, or a priority on commercial outcomes over actual project success. A signed contract, no matter how detailed, cannot by itself mobilise individuals to work effectively together within a truly collaborative framework.
The Hidden Problem: Contracts Don't Guarantee Collaboration

Most project managers assume a signed contract marks the beginning of execution. In reality, it often marks the moment when structural barriers emerge that prevent teams from acting . Brett Ackroyd, a commercial lawyer with 26 years of experience on defence and government mega-projects, explains that contractual language addresses only one dimension of project delivery—the legal one.

The real failure mechanism is more subtle. Teams possess the knowledge and capability to solve problems, but organisational boundaries, lack of cross-functional authority, and competing commercial incentives create paralysis. A developer knows how to fix a design flaw; a supply chain manager sees a cost-saving opportunity; a partner identifies a risk—yet none act, because the contract, the hierarchy, or the fear of liability stops them first.

As Ackroyd discusses in the podcast , this isn't a training or communication problem. It's a systemic one embedded in how organisations structure relationships and incentives around projects. When people prioritise protecting their contractual position over advancing the collective outcome, the project—not the contract—suffers the consequences.

This shift from reactive crisis management to predictive problem-solving is fundamentally about relationship clarity. From reactive delays to predictive delivery

Scottish Water's comparative research was telling: projects that had invested in building collaborative working relationships cut their delay times dramatically. The difference wasn't about better technology, more budget, or longer schedules—it was purely about relationship certainty enabling anticipation .

When a problem emerges on a collaborative project, teams don't spend time negotiating blame, checking contracts, or waiting for sign-off from distant stakeholders. They already know how their partner operates, what trade-offs they'll accept, and what the shared priority actually is. A potential five-day delay becomes a one-day adjustment.

Why personal relationships alone will fail you

Most project failures happen not during contract negotiation, but after the contract is signed . When relationships exist only between individuals, the entire project delivery depends on their continued presence and goodwill. Remove one person, and the foundation crumbles.

Building systems that outlast individuals

ISO 44001 is the framework most project leaders have never heard of but should have. It provides a structured approach to collaborative relationship management, embedding values and behaviours into organisational systems rather than personalities.

ee2384c227.q: What is the difference between minimum viable governance and minimum governance?

f: Minimum viable governance is not about doing less—it's about doing exactly what's needed . It means creating structures and systems that enable the right people to make the right decisions at the right time to manage project risk, calibrated precisely to the project's actual risk profile, not its budget.
The core misconception: less is not the goal

The term "minimum viable" often gets confused with "minimal," but as Isabel Grae Garaway explains in the episode , they are fundamentally different. Minimum viable governance is about fitness for purpose—creating governance that fits the actual needs of the project, not creating the least governance possible.

Think of it this way: a quarter-million-dollar project and a half-million-dollar project may require different governance structures entirely , not simply less governance. The difference lies in understanding what risk actually exists and what decision-making architecture is required to manage it effectively.
Governance scaled to risk, not to budget

The critical principle is that governance should be relative to risk . If the risk is low, governance ideally should be low to reflect that. If the risk is high, governance must rise to meet it. The mistake most organizations make is either applying one-size-fits-all governance or stripping it away entirely because they think it slows delivery.

afc7fad568.q: How can governance structures be designed to prevent project delivery failure before a project even starts?
afc7fad568.a: Clear sponsorship with executive accountability is the foundation. If you do not have a clear sponsor and clear executive accountability, you are doomed to…

f: Project failure is predictable before execution even begins. If a project lacks clear sponsorship with explicit executive accountability , it is fundamentally compromised from the start. Five structural elements must be locked in place before launch: uncontested scope definition, an articulated business case with intended benefits, secured budget, organizational change readiness assessment, and robust governance scaled to the real risk profile.
Governance precedes failure, not the reverse

Isabel Grae Garaway emphasizes that governance always precedes delivery failure. The problem is not that governance fails during execution—it is that the failure was already embedded in weak governance decisions made before the project even launched. Weak sponsorship, undefined scope, or misaligned budget are not obstacles to fix mid-project; they are red flags that the project was never properly chartered.

As Garaway explores in the episode , the governance structure must reflect the actual risk level of the project. Too much governance creates bureaucratic drag; too little leaves critical decisions unmade. The goal is fit-for-purpose governance —exactly the right level of structure and decision authority to enable the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.
Five non-negotiable governance foundations

The first foundation is clear sponsorship and executive accountability . Without a named sponsor who owns the outcome and commands enough organizational authority to remove obstacles, the project is already set up to fail. Accountability must be personal and visible, not diffused across a committee.

59f2202fea.q: What is the core difference between managing under pressure and leading under pressure in project management?
59f2202fea.a: Managing under pressure means you are doing okay yourself, but leading under pressure means that you are helping everyone else get through that phase as well. The distinction is critical because as a project manager, you need to remain calm and provide clarity and direction to your team even when facing severe financial, time, personnel, or third-party pressures.
59f2202fea.e: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
f: Managing under pressure means you are handling your own performance adequately, but leading under pressure means you are actively helping your team navigate difficult phases as well. As a project manager, staying calm and providing clarity and direction to your team remains essential even when facing severe financial, time, personnel, or third-party pressures.

The distinction matters because many project managers conflate coping with crisis with actually leading their team through it. You might be meeting your own deadlines and maintaining your composure, yet if your team is confused, demoralised, or left without clear direction, you're only managing yourself—not leading.

Nick Jagger, whose 45 years of project management experience spans major infrastructure projects including work as a risk manager on the $8 billion Northwest Ruralink (later Sydney Metro), emphasises that this shift from managing to leading is fundamental. The technical aspects of the role—schedules, budgets, scope—pale in comparison to how you hold the space for your people during crisis.

Real leadership under pressure involves communicating with transparency . Your team needs to understand what constraints exist, what options remain on the table, and what you expect from them. Without that clarity, pressure cascades downward as anxiety rather than focus.
"It is not necessarily what the project manager knows that makes the difference. It is how they can work with the team."

Nick Jagger — Technical Director of Project Management, Elemental Projects. 2b9ce19d53.q: How has the role of project manager evolved from the 1950s to today?
2b9ce19d53.a: Project managers were originally the most senior technical person with deep expertise in the specific field, such as a senior bridge engineer managing bridge construction. Over 70 years, the role shifted to being an expert in stakeholder engagement, communication, and soft skills rather than technical expertise. The discipline moved from accidental project managers, who shuffled into the role after reaching technical mastery, to intentional project managers who actively choose and study project management as a desirable career.
2b9ce19d53.e: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
f: The project manager role transformed from a technical position filled by the most senior expert in a field into a leadership role centered on stakeholder engagement and soft skills. What was once an accidental career path—technical professionals who naturally became project managers after reaching mastery—evolved into an intentional discipline that professionals actively choose and study from the start.
From Senior Engineer to People Leader

In the 1950s and 1960s, when the term "project manager" was first coined, the role belonged to the most experienced technical specialist in the room —a senior bridge engineer overseeing bridge construction, or the most skilled person in any given field. These were accidental project managers, people who had climbed so high in their technical expertise that project leadership fell to them naturally.

This model assumed that deep technical knowledge was the foundation of leadership. The project manager's authority came from knowing more about the work than anyone else on the team. Over seven decades, this premise inverted entirely. As Nick Jagger explains in the episode , the discipline shifted to prioritizing expertise in communication, stakeholder engagement, and emotional intelligence over technical depth.
"It is not necessarily what the project manager knows that makes the difference. It is how they can work with the team."

Nick Jagger — Technical Director of Project Management at Elemental Projects. A project management veteran with 45 years of experience who moved from England to Australia in 2008, Jagger studied a Masters of Project Management at UTS and worked on major infrastructure projects including the $8 billion Northwest Ruralink (later Sydney Metro) as a risk manager at ACOM. After approximately 10 years with ACOM, he moved to smaller consultancy Ontwit focusing on social infrastructure, then joined Mark McDonald as technical director, and has spent the last 18 months at Elemental Projects, a registered training organisation delivering project management and leadership training.

477203c3b9.q: What is the core definition of governance in project delivery, and how does it differ from administration and project management?
477203c3b9.a: Governance is the structure and systems that ensure the right people make the right decisions at the right time about project and delivery risk. It is fundamentally about transparency, accountability, and how risk is treated through organized timeframes. Administration, project management, micromanagement, and policing are not governance—they are supporting activities. Governance is not committees, meetings, minutes, templates, or risk registers; those are instruments, but governance itself is enabling decision-making, not theatre.

15ce652197.q: How does the RoboDebt program exemplify governance failure in public sector delivery?
15ce652197.a: RoboDebt (2015–2019) was a governance failure, not a technology or data failure. It lacked a single accountable executive decision maker, with multiple agencies and ministers overseeing the program. Risk registers were not kept updated, frontline staff escalations about incorrect numbers and traumatized citizens were ignored, and legal concerns about the legality of the process were not escalated to senior executives. The governance structures existed but were not followed, and in the absence of executive accountability, the program team filled decision-making gaps without proper oversight, contributing to the program's spectacular failure.
15ce652197.e: Your Project Didn't Fail. Your Governance Did. | Ep. 14
f: RoboDebt (2015–2019) failed because no single executive held accountability for decision-making, despite governance structures being in place. Risk registers went unreviewed, frontline staff warnings about incorrect calculations were ignored, and legal concerns were never escalated to senior decision-makers—the machinery of governance existed, but nobody actually used it.

The RoboDebt story reveals a crucial distinction: governance failure is not the same as the absence of governance structures. The Australian government had all the formal frameworks in place—committees, risk registers, audit trails, oversight bodies. What was missing was the will to enforce them .

Multiple agencies and ministers shared responsibility, which meant nobody felt fully accountable. When a steering committee meets but produces zero decisions, as Isabel Gray-Garraway explains in the podcast , the project team fills the void with guesswork and pushes forward unsupervised. That's exactly what happened: the RoboDebt team operated in a decision-making vacuum, making critical choices without proper executive sign-off.

Frontline staff—the people closest to the data and the harm being caused—raised alarms about incorrect numbers and traumatized citizens. These escalations never reached the top. Risk signals were systematically ignored , not because they were hidden, but because nobody with real power was listening.
When governance theatre masks absence of accountability

The RoboDebt failure cost the Australian government close to $2 billion in refunds, repayments, reimbursements, and compensation . A Royal Commission wasn't held until 2023, three years after the program ended. Six years later, the reputational damage persists.

RoboDebt (2015–2019) represents not merely a failed program, but the most significant failure in public administration in modern Australian history . The scale of the financial consequence—nearly $2 billion in direct payouts—reflects the depth of governance breakdown that allowed the system to operate unchecked.

As Isabel Gray-Garraway explains in the episode , governance failures of this magnitude don't resolve quickly. Three years after RoboDebt ended, a Royal Commission was formally convened in 2023 to investigate how such a systematic failure had occurred and persisted within government systems.
A failure that rewrote Australian governance history

The reputational wound runs deeper than typical program failures. RoboDebt has become shorthand for government overreach without accountability —a reference point invoked in media coverage and public discourse whenever authorities propose new digital systems or automated decision-making processes. The program's legacy is one of institutional mistrust.

This lasting damage matters beyond optics. When a government program becomes synonymous with administrative failure, it affects public confidence in future government initiatives. The fact that RoboDebt remains a mainstream media reference six years later—and counting—demonstrates that the consequences of poor governance extend well beyond the program's closure , influencing policy acceptance and public trust in subsequent announcements.

9878db7e7b.q: Why does good governance often have a poor reputation while bad governance is highly memorable?
9878db7e7b.a: Good governance is invisible because it works seamlessly—processes flow together, decisions are made, project teams feel supported, and it becomes business as usual. Bad governance is unforgettable because people remember negative experiences far longer than positive ones. In office environments, people compete to share worst-governance stories rather than celebrating when governance works well. This creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where poor governance experiences carry forward to future projects and organizations, shaping negative expectations and organizational culture around governance.
9878db7e7b.e: Your Project Didn't Fail. Your Governance Did. | Ep. 14
f: Good governance is invisible because it works seamlessly —processes flow together, decisions are made, project teams feel supported, and it becomes business as usual. Bad governance is unforgettable because people remember negative experiences far longer than positive ones, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy where poor governance shapes organizational culture for years to come.
The Visibility Gap: Why Success Goes Unnoticed

When governance functions properly, no one talks about it. Teams receive clear decision-making authority, risk is managed transparently, and stakeholders know who decides what and when. The system becomes so routine that its effectiveness disappears into the background. This invisibility is actually governance working as intended —it enables delivery rather than impeding it.

In contrast, as Isabel Gray-Garraway explains in the episode , bad governance creates friction that people actively notice and discuss. Steering committees produce zero decisions. Project teams guess their way forward. Accountability vanishes. These experiences stick in organizational memory far more powerfully than smooth delivery ever does.
The Storytelling Problem: Offices as Gossip Networks

In office environments, people don't gather to celebrate when governance works. They compete to share worst-governance stories with colleagues, reinforcing a shared narrative of dysfunction. One person recalls a project where unclear authority delayed decisions for months. Another describes a steering committee that never actually decided anything. These anecdotes spread, shaping how new employees and incoming leaders perceive governance long before they experience it firsthand.

7bde6ed6ac.q: How does poor governance experience transfer across organizations and impact future project outcomes?
7bde6ed6ac.a: Negative governance experiences are transferable across time and organizations. When people move to a new organization three years after a poor experience, they carry that negative experience with them and may already be on the back foot. En masse, poor experiences create a self-fulfilling prophecy around governance. Organizations develop bad reputations around governance that stick like mud, regardless of what executives say, because language and actions are behaviors. This organizational perception becomes deeply embedded in culture and carries forward to new projects and initiatives.
7bde6ed6ac.e: Your Project Didn't Fail. Your Governance Did. | Ep. 14
f: Negative governance experiences are transferable across time and organizations —when people move to a new organization years after a poor experience, they carry that baggage with them. En masse, these bad experiences create a self-fulfilling prophecy around governance, embedding organizational reputations so deeply in culture that they persist regardless of what executives actually say or do.
How negative experiences become organizational identity

The damage doesn't reset when someone changes roles or companies. A person who experienced poor governance at one organization brings those scars forward, already skeptical and defensive before they even begin. Organizations develop reputations around governance that stick like mud , not because they lack good intentions, but because reputation is built on visible, lived behavior—not on aspirational messaging.

This is where the gap between language and action becomes critical. Executives can declare that governance has improved, that systems have changed, and that decision-making is now fit for purpose. But as Isabel Gray-Garraway discusses in the episode , the real signal is what people actually experience when they work through those governance structures day to day.
Culture embeds past failures into future projects

Once a governance failure happens—especially one visible across an entire organization or sector—that perception becomes embedded in organizational culture. New projects inherit that skepticism. Team members approach governance processes already expecting them to fail or obstruct, making it harder to rebuild trust even when structures genuinely improve.

40bafffa4b.q: What role did confusion between governance and policing play in RoboDebt's punitive outcomes?
40bafffa4b.a: The program team and stakeholders believed in the governance structures, but the way governance was executed from a technology and process perspective became policing. Because policing and governance became misconstrued as one, the program became punitive to people theoretically owing money to the Australian government. This confusion around punitive governance actions is what gave RoboDebt its terrible reputation. The Australian public remembers RoboDebt with an associated terrible reputation specifically because of the punitive nature of the program and its outcomes.
40bafffa4b.e: Your Project Didn't Fail. Your Governance Did. | Ep. 14
f: The RoboDebt program collapsed because governance structures and policing actions became indistinguishable —what should have been oversight became punishment. When the program team executed governance through technology and process in ways that felt punitive to citizens, the line between legitimate control and harassment vanished, cementing a reputation that persists years later.

The distinction between governance and policing is subtle but critical. Governance exists to ensure the right people make informed decisions about risk at the right time. When executed properly, it creates clarity and trust. But in RoboDebt, the mechanisms meant to oversee and manage the program transformed into something far more aggressive—citizens experienced governance actions as direct punitive enforcement against them personally.

This shift happened not because anyone explicitly decided to punish people, but because the program's technology and process design blurred the boundary. As Isabel Gray-Garraway explains in the episode , the stakeholders and program team believed genuinely in the governance structure they had created. The intent was sound. Yet the execution—the algorithms, the automated letters, the debt recovery mechanisms—landed on citizens as coercive rather than corrective.

Isabel Gray-Garraway — Director of ICT Corporate Portfolio at Fire and Rescue NSW, with 25 years of project delivery experience across defence, government, and public-private hybrid organisations. She spent 17 years in government roles learning the relationship between risk, accountability, and governance. She led a 100-person team managing a $200 million rolling program at Transport for New South Wales.

The consequences were profound. The Australian public remembers RoboDebt not as a flawed governance system but as a punitive program targeting vulnerable people . This perception gap—between what was intended as oversight and what was experienced as persecution—damaged public trust in government institutions far beyond the program itself. The Royal Commission held three years after RoboDebt ended found the governance failures so severe that the government ultimately spent close to $2 billion on refunds, repayments, reimbursements, and compensation.

What makes this case instructive is that the confusion between governance and policing was not inevitable. It emerged from how governance was operationalized—from the technical systems chosen, the process flows designed, and the absence of human judgment at critical intervention points. The full episode explores how organizations can redesign governance structures to remain oversight-focused rather than drifting into enforcement, and why this distinction matters for both project outcomes and public confidence.
